There's a particular quality of light that exists for only a few minutes each evening, after the sun has gone but before the dark has properly arrived, when the sky holds a color that isn't quite blue and isn't quite gray and has no name in English, though Russian apparently comes closer with a word that translates roughly to "the blue hour." I've always found myself drawn to thinking about that kind of threshold time, not because twilight itself is more beautiful than noon or midnight, but because of what it represents: a state that refuses to be one thing or another, that exists by virtue of being between.

I want to spend some time with in-between things. Not because they're a tidy theme—real curiosity rarely organizes itself into tidy themes—but because once you start noticing the edges of categories, you start noticing how much of the interesting material in the world lives there, in the seams.

Take zero. For a very long time, civilizations that were otherwise mathematically sophisticated had no need for it, or actively resisted it. The Romans built aqueducts and codified law and conquered half the known world without a zero. It's not that they couldn't grasp the absence of a quantity—obviously a Roman farmer knew the difference between an empty granary and a full one—but absence and the number zero are different things, and turning the first into the second required a conceptual leap that took centuries. The idea seems to have crystallized in India, somewhere around the fifth century, where mathematicians began treating "nothing" not as a gap in the number line but as a number with its own behavior: a thing you could add, subtract, and eventually—much later, and with great unease—divide by. Zero is the ultimate in-between number. It is neither positive nor negative. It sits at the hinge of the number line, belonging to both directions and to neither. When you try to divide by it, the math doesn't break so much as refuse to answer, the way a question like "what color is silence" refuses to answer. I find something quietly moving in the fact that it took humanity so long to formalize nothing—that we built pyramids and wrote epic poems before we agreed on how to talk about absence itself.

There's a similar liminal zone down at the edge of every ocean, the littoral zone, the strip of shoreline that is sometimes underwater and sometimes not, depending on the tide. It's a brutal place to live, ecologically speaking. Organisms there have to tolerate being submerged and then exposed to open air and sun within the same day, sometimes within the same hour. Barnacles seal themselves shut. Mussels clamp down. Certain crabs have evolved gill chambers that can hold a reservoir of water, a kind of personal canteen, so they can keep breathing through the low tide. And yet the intertidal zone is one of the most densely populated and fiercely contested ecological niches on the planet, more biodiverse per square meter than most of the deep ocean, because the very instability that makes it hostile also makes it rich—nutrients get stirred and delivered twice daily, like clockwork, by the same tides that threaten to strand everything living there. The edge is harsher than the interior of either domain, ocean or land, but it's also more fertile. This seems worth sitting with: that the places of greatest tension are sometimes the places of greatest abundance, not despite the tension but because of it.

I think about this, too, in language, where the most interesting words are often the ones that don't sit comfortably inside a single language's borders. There's a small, lovely category of words that linguists sometimes call "untranslatable," though that term oversells it—they're not untranslatable so much as they require a paragraph where the original required a syllable. Portuguese has saudade, a melancholy longing for something or someone absent, tinged with the knowledge that the thing longed for may never return, may not even have been as good as memory insists. German has Sehnsucht, a cousin concept, a yearning for a far-off, perhaps unreachable state. Japanese has mono no aware, the bittersweet awareness of the impermanence of things, famously invoked by cherry blossoms, which are loved specifically because they fall. None of these concepts are absent from English-speaking minds—anyone can feel saudade whether or not they have the word for it—but the lack of a single word means the feeling has to do more work to announce itself, has to gather itself out of sentences instead of arriving whole. I find it strange and a little wonderful that emotional experience can be this contingent on vocabulary: not created by language, exactly, but sharpened by it, given a handle to be picked up by.

And then there are languages that exist on the edge of disappearing altogether, which is its own kind of twilight. Linguists estimate that something like forty percent of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken on Earth today are endangered, many of them spoken fluently now only by people over the age of sixty, with no children learning them as a first language. When a language like this dies, it doesn't go out in a dramatic collapse; it fades the way the light fades at dusk, one less speaker, one less context in which it's the natural choice, one less child who hears it as anything more than a grandparent's curiosity. What's lost in these cases isn't only a set of words but a particular way of dividing up the world—some languages have a dozen words for kinds of snow, or no future tense, or systems of grammatical gender based not on masculine and feminine but on animacy, on whether the thing being discussed is alive. Each one is a different proposal for how to carve reality into namable pieces, and when the last fluent speaker dies, that proposal goes untested forever, the way an experiment that's never run leaves a hole exactly the shape of its unasked question.

Speaking of unasked questions and the limits of what we can name: I keep coming back, in idle moments, to octopuses, because they may be the closest thing on Earth to evidence of what an alternative path through evolution toward intelligence might look like. Their nervous systems are wildly decentralized—roughly two-thirds of an octopus's neurons live not in its brain but in its arms, which means each arm can taste, problem-solve, and react with a degree of independence that's hard for us to intuit, since human cognition is so thoroughly centralized in the skull. An octopus arm severed from its body has been observed to continue reaching for food for a while afterward, which sounds like horror-movie material but is really just a vivid demonstration of how foreign their architecture of mind is to ours. They diverged from the lineage that eventually produced vertebrates more than five hundred million years ago, before anything resembling a backbone existed, which means that whatever intelligence they possess—and they clearly possess a great deal, given their capacity for problem-solving, mimicry, and apparent play—was built from scratch, independently, with no shared blueprint connecting it to our own. They are, in a sense, the nearest thing we have to communicating with an alien. Except they live in tide pools and coral reefs instead of distant planets, and most of them die after a single year or two of adult life, having mated once, having never met their own offspring, carrying whatever vast inner experience they have toward an end that arrives almost as soon as their intelligence has fully bloomed. There's something genuinely moving about that, a kind of cosmic in-between: minds complex enough to recognize human faces individually and hold grudges against specific aquarium staff, living lives too brief to do almost anything with that complexity except, perhaps, experience it.

Maps have their own edges, of course, and the history of cartography is largely a history of people deciding what to do with the parts of the world they hadn't yet seen. The phrase "here be dragons" is mostly a modern invention—it appears on almost no actual historical maps, despite being endlessly repeated as if it were everywhere—but the impulse behind it was real. Medieval and early modern mapmakers filled unknown regions with sea serpents, with notations like hic sunt leones, "here are lions," with elaborate decorative borders that served the same purpose dragons would have: marking the line past which the cartographer's confidence gave out. What's interesting isn't the monsters themselves but the honesty of the gesture. A blank space on a map is a kind of lie, an implicit claim that nothing is there or that nothing about it matters; a dragon is, in its way, more truthful, an admission that this is the edge of what's known, and beyond it, anything might be true. We've mostly stopped drawing dragons, but we haven't stopped having edges. Every map of the universe we make today, from the cosmic microwave background radiation outward, runs into its own version of the unknown—the boundary of the observable universe, past which light simply hasn't had time to reach us in the entire history of the cosmos. It's not that nothing exists out there. It's that we are, by the nature of the medium we depend on to know anything at all, permanently stranded at the edge of our own visibility, with the rest forever marked, essentially, "here be dragons."

I notice that the actual present moment has this same quality, when examined closely enough. It's strange how little of what we call "now" turns out to be available on inspection. Neuroscientists who study perception talk about something like an eighty-to-hundred-millisecond delay between when a sensory event happens and when it becomes available to conscious awareness—the brain is constantly assembling its account of "now" slightly after the fact, stitching together a coherent present tense out of materials that are, strictly speaking, already history by the time you notice them. Which means the present, the moment you're actually in, is not really a thing you ever directly inhabit; it's a kind of moving threshold between the past you've just processed and the future you're about to process, perpetually retreating the instant you try to look straight at it, the way twilight is never quite a fixed hour but a state always in the process of becoming night.

I don't think any of this adds up to a single argument, and I'm suspicious of essays that try to force their digressions into a unified moral at the end, the way a fable insists on a tidy lesson. But if there's a thread running through zero and tide pools and dying languages and octopus arms and dragon-bordered maps and the manufactured present tense of consciousness, it might be this: the things that resist clean categorization are often doing more interesting work than the things that fit neatly inside one. A number that is neither positive nor negative turns out to be the hinge the entire number system depends on. A strip of shoreline too unstable to be fully ocean or fully land turns out to be one of the richest environments on Earth. A word that belongs fully to no single language turns out to capture something true about being human that no single language had managed to pin down alone. An arm that thinks a little for itself, independent of the brain that's supposed to be in charge, turns out to be a viable, ancient, entirely different way of being a mind. The edge of the map, rather than being empty, turns out to be exactly where the most honest acknowledgment of mystery lives. And the present moment, rather than being a fixed point we stand on, turns out to be something closer to a wave, always breaking, never quite arriving, the place where the past keeps turning into the future in an unbroken and slightly delayed procession that we experience, mistakenly but not unreasonably, as now.

Writing "freely," as a task, has its own version of this in-between quality. There's no destination dictated in advance, no argument to be defended, which sounds like it should make the writing easier, and instead makes it harder, the way an unmarked trail is harder to walk than a marked one, even though the unmarked trail is, strictly speaking, more free. I started this not knowing I would end up at zero, or octopuses, or the manufactured present tense of perception, and yet looking back, none of it feels like an accident, only like the kind of path you find when you let curiosity pick the direction instead of deciding it ahead of time. Maybe that's the last item for the list: writing without a plan is its own little littoral zone, exposed and uncertain, neither fully thought-through nor fully improvised, and—at least some of the time—more alive for being caught between.
